title: Swedish Historical Calendar
intro: For a short period, Sweden used calendar dates that were not quite the Julian dates and not yet Gregorian dates. Its unusual reform even created 30 February 1712, a date that sounds impossible today.
diagram_caption: THREE MILESTONES IN SWEDEN'S CALENDAR CHANGE
caption_detail: Swedish dates were shifted by an abandoned reform, then put back into the Julian system before the final Gregorian switch.

steps.heading: 1700: Sweden begins a gradual change
steps.text: Sweden planned to move from Julian to Gregorian reckoning by skipping leap days. It skipped the Julian leap day in 1700, leaving its calendar one day ahead of Julian dates.

steps.heading: 1712: the extra day
steps.text: The plan was abandoned and the Julian reckoning restored. Sweden added an extra day in February 1712, producing the genuinely historical date 30 February.

steps.heading: 1753: a sudden Gregorian change
steps.text: Sweden finally switched to the Gregorian calendar by moving directly from Wednesday 17 February 1753 to Thursday 1 March 1753 in its civil date labels. Eleven numbered dates were omitted.

example: In the local Swedish sequence, 29 February 1712 was followed by 30 February 1712 and then 1 March 1712. In 1753, 17 February was followed immediately by 1 March: there was no local 18-28 February that year.
history: European countries changed from the older Julian calendar to the Gregorian calendar on different dates. Sweden attempted a gradual transition in 1700, reversed its change in 1712 and finally adopted Gregorian date labels in 1753.
model: The provider models Sweden's documented 1700-1753 exceptions: Julian labels before the reform, the unusual 1712 leap correction and the 1753 Gregorian switch. It does not introduce a fictional everlasting Swedish calendar.
limits: Modern dates and historical Swedish dates cannot be compared by label alone around the reform. The Swedish historical date numbering is a defined local rule; different neighbouring countries may have labelled the same physical day differently.
